When I do this my pain diminishes immensely over a short period, sometimes as short as an hour or so. If I'm only in my mind, though, I am bound to remember the memory and do something about it, even if it isn't a healthy one. The more I think about it the harder and longer it becomes to get it out of my mind, though. It takes many, many hours and, to this point, the memory has not fully dissipated. It hasn't disappeared completely—it still gets triggered by things I read or hear—so there's still lingering, ugly thoughts about everything I've said or done or didn't do. It still hurts to think about. Sometimes I feel sick to my stomach thinking about it, and that scares me. If I can get through it for a few hours it goes away, and I can go back to having an ordinary day again. But if not, it will never go away. It will be there the next day and the next, and I can't get rid of it. It's like living with a deep, buried and painful memory; it just keeps returning.

Mzilikazi High School^{[1]} is a State school located in Matabeleland North province in Zimbabwe in the town of Zhombe. It is located in Insiza District. The school was founded in 1969.

## Introduction[edit]

The school was opened in 1969 by the newly independent Rhodesia (renamed Zimbabwe) as a boarding school. It was founded and given its name as a tribute to Mzilikazi Khumalo, a Nguni king, founder and first ruler of the Matabele nation, who lived in what is known today as the Zimbabwe. The school originally began as a co-educational boarding school, with both male and female students living in two separate dormitories. In the 1980s, most of the female students left and the school became exclusively a boys school for grade seven and onwards. The school has produced Rhodes scholar and Moto Lokwe, founder of the Zimbabwe Broadcasting Company as well as several MPs, ministers and other notable people in Zimbabwe.

## Academic record[edit]

The school has been a high performing school throughout its relatively short history winning numerous awards (best in district, second in province and best in district. It has been consistently placed in the best 30 schools in Zimbabwe and has several notable alumni.

- Tongai Mnangagwa, businessman and MP
- Aiden Ndlovu, MP for the Zapu party
- Moto Lokwe, Founder of the Zimbabwe broadcaster
- Shadreck Mashayamombe, Minister of Transport and Communications.

Jacques Boyceau (1607 â€“ 1642) was a French organist and composer who became a monk of the Congregation of Saint-Maur in 1631. He is best known for his compositions for organ and for theorbo and several of his works were published during his lifetime in Paris, 1632, Lyon, 1639, and Lyons 1646. He also authored a treatise on the organ Le jeu de l'orgue plainte-pleureuse which has become very rare.
The most important of his organ music was the "Messe brÃ¨ve" (Missa brevis) in A minor published in the Mascaroton collection of organ music. This mass is especially interesting because it is for a small organ with only four stops. Boyceau also composed for theorbo and published several sets of Pieces de ThordÃ¨be in 1632 and 1645 for two and for three instruments (or instruments and organ). The music is especially noteworthy as it was published in separate parts for treble (bass is not specified) and for bass with figured bass.
In addition to his organ, theorbo and chamber works, Boyceau wrote liturgical music, including an "office" for Saint-Maur which remained unpublished during his lifetime. It is also worth noting that Boyceau was active as a teacher and was the teacher of Jacques Lemoyne the Younger and of the composer Claude Achard.[1]

"Empty Rooms" is a term often used in various contexts such as literature, art, psychology, and philosophy for various symbolic and metaphorical interpretations. As a physical or conceptual space, an 'empty room' carries various interpretations ranging from solitude, void, potential, reflection, or infinite possibilities.

In Literature and Art

The concept of an 'empty room' serves as a powerful metaphor in literature and art. Many authors and artists have used it to symbolize potential, loneliness, change, or the human condition. For example, Virginia Woolf's novel "To the Room" and Edward Hopper's painting "Room in New York" explore various themes using the metaphor of an empty room. 

In Film and Music

Empty rooms have also played prominent roles in cinema and music. These include the song "Empty Rooms" by Gary Moore, and the film "The Empty Room", a German drama film directed by Ralf Marschalleck. In these, the room stands as a silent witness to the events unfolding, echoing the loneliness and the void.

In Psychology

From a psychological perspective, an 'empty room' often symbolizes a mental state or a particular condition. Carl Jung, for instance, talked about 'empty rooms' in his works, signifying areas of the mind where individuals need to do inner work to understand unconscious elements of their personality.

In Philosophy

Philosophers often use the concept of the 'empty room' in exploring existential questions. Absence or nothingness questions the meaning of existence, speaking to the core of existential philosophy. 

Architecture and Design

In architecture and interior design, an empty room signals limitless potential. It becomes a canvas on which architects and designers can project their visions. It is also frequently used as a concept in minimalistic designing emphasizing simplicity and functionality over clutter and excess. 

Virtual Technology

In the realm of virtual technology, 'empty room' is a term used to describe a virtual environment yet to be populated by objects or people. 

While an empty room might seem to signify nothingness, it is in this space that creativity often springs. It holds a significant position as a metaphor across diverse disciplines, evoking various themes and emotions. Just like a painter sees a blank canvas, the endless interpretations of an 'empty room' are a testament to the human ability to perceive, interpret, and assign meanings. 

See also:
* Negative Space
* Cognitive psychology
* Existentialism
* Minimalist architecture

Raspberry Linzer Cookies

"These are a great cookie for the holidays. They are a little time consuming, but well worth the effort. The raspberry jam in the center is a nice surprise."

Ingredients

1 cup butter, softened

1 cup sugar

2 eggs

1 teaspoon vanilla extract

2 cups all-purpose flour

1/2 teaspoon salt

1/2 teaspoon baking powder

1/2 teaspoon baking soda

1/2 cup raspberry jam

Directions

1. Preheat oven to 350 degrees F (175 degrees C).

2. In a large bowl, cream together the butter and sugar until smooth. Beat in the eggs one at a time, then stir in the vanilla. Combine the flour, salt, baking powder and baking soda; gradually add to the creamed mixture and mix well.

3. Roll out half of the dough on a lightly floured surface to 1/8-inch thickness. Cut out cookies using a 2-inch round cookie cutter. Place on ungreased baking sheets.

4. Spoon 1/2 teaspoon of jam into the center of each cookie.

5. Roll out remaining dough to 1/8-inch thickness. Cut out cookies using a 2-inch round cookie cutter. Place over the jam on the first cookies.

6. Bake for 10 to 12 minutes in the preheated oven, or until lightly browned. Cool on wire racks.

Yield: about 2 dozen.

An adaptive thresholding technique is then applied to optimize the separation between regions, ensuring that each region contains pixels with consistent color characteristics.

The adaptive thresholding mechanism allows the algorithm to automatically adjust the level of detail in the segmentation, enabling it to capture both local and global features of the image.

Experiments conducted on several benchmark datasets demonstrate the superiority of VRAUS compared to state-of-the-art unsupervised segmentation methods. Additionally, we perform a series of parameter studies to analyze the impact of different components of the algorithm and provide insights into their role in achieving optimal performance.

* The proposal of a novel unsupervised color image segmentation algorithm, VRAUS, that combines the benefits of Voronoi regions and adaptive thresholding.

Edmund Ashton Baillieu, known as Ted Baillieu, (born 31 July 1953) is an Australian politician who served as 46th Premier of Victoria. Born and raised in Melbourne, Ted Baillieu was educated at Melbourne Grammar School and the University of Melbourne where he graduated with degrees in architecture and commerce. Before entering politics, he had a successful career in property and business.

Baillieu secured his foothold in politics as a member of the Victorian Legislative Assembly for Hawthorn in 1999 - a position that he held until 2014. His political trajectory experienced a notable incline when he was elected Leader of the Victorian Liberal Party in 2006.

During his term as Premier, Baillieu implemented several reformative projects that spanned a wide array of sectors. His focus areas included education, infrastructure, healthcare, and law enforcement. His leadership was largely characterized by fiscal conservatism and a strong emphasis on sustainable development.

Some of Baillieu's staple achievements were the establishment of Protective Services Officers at Victorian train stations, reforms in public health sector, a boost in infrastructure spending, and the implementation of the Victorian Bushfires Royal Commission’s recommendations.

In March 2013, Baillieu resigned as Premier of Victoria in the face of ongoing leadership tensions within the Liberal Party. He was succeeded by Denis Napthine. Baillieu ran successfully again as a member of the Victorian Parliament in the 2014 state election, but did not seek re-election in 2018. Post political career, Baillieu continues his work in architecture and business, with a particular focus on sustainable development.

On a personal note, Ted Baillieu is married to Robyn Baillieu, with whom he has three children. Baillieu is not only recognized for his political and business acumen, but also for his involvement in various philanthropic activities throughout his career. He remains a formidable figure in Australian politics and business circles.

And while it certainly has many flaws, 'Alexander' isn't the total failure many claim it to be. The film benefits immensely from the sheer ambition of its scope and vision; it may not be entirely successful, but Stone's Athens-to-India extravaganza certainly isn't lacking in ambition. Numerous sweeping wide shots of armies marching into battle dwarf the actors, as do the frequent CGI shots of elephants and horses, eventually resulting in a somewhat chaotic but always intriguing canvas. The film feels like 'Ben-Hur' meets 'Lord of the Rings,' and while the former may be considered the more successful of the two, it's Stone's ambition and unique vision that make 'Alexander' worth a look.

Stone, who also wrote the script, draws heavily from both history and fiction, borrowing from the epics of Homer, the ancient Greek playwright, and the King James Bible, among other sources. The result is a script that meanders through history, acting as a loose backdrop for the film's visual spectacle. The story opens in 343 BC as Alexander's father, King Philip II of Macedonia (a stiff performance from Brian Cox) is about to engage the Greek city of Athens in battle, ultimately resulting in his victory and the city's destruction. Once, I saw myself in a mirror.
In the reflection, I saw all the things I should do to make
myself more appealing: I saw that I should try and be
different from the rest, I have to do something that would
make me unique.
My parents said I was too short for my age;
I will have to work on my figure. I should learn to walk
and talk like someone more attractive,
I have to be different and be someone in particular.
I got a piece of paper and a pen to make a list of priorities.
But then, I began to wonder why do I need to look different.
Then I began to doubt if I need to walk like someone prettier.
I began to doubt the things that I needed to do to be someone else.
I suddenly felt a sense of insecurity;
I wondered what if I could not do all those things?
I then looked in the mirror, I began to ask myself what am I afraid of?
My father always advised me to be a better person,
But I do not know if I really have to change my personality and my nature
just to follow my parent's advice.
Just then, I felt the need to express my true self,
And I began to wish that people really understood my real self,
Even when I make a mistake.
When I realize that I should truly be myself,
I was finally able to accept my flaws and be someone who I always wanted to be.
Only then, I realized that I should truly be contented with my actual self,
Not be someone else by changing my personality,
Instead, I started to love my flaws and accept my mistakes
until I eventually realized that I was always a better person
than I thought I was in the first place.

A new, pocket-sized device could help people with hearing loss communicate more easily with others.

The phone, called Sign, is being developed by a team at Harvard University's Wyss Institute, along with a Boston-based startup called MotionSavvy.

The device consists of a tablet with a screen the size of a smartphone, attached to a base that contains a camera.

That camera tracks the movements of the user's hands, allowing them to communicate in sign language.

The team at Harvard, who developed the technology, say it is the first time sign language has been translated into text and then spoken aloud, all in real time.

They hope it will make life easier for the estimated 36 million people in the US alone whose hearing is impaired.

The Sign device translates sign language into text, which it then speaks aloud, helping deaf people communicate with the hearing.

It does this through a sophisticated algorithm that can track hands and identify letters.

"It's a communication barrier that this technology breaks down," said MotionSavvy CEO Alex Dreger.

"It's a tool that lets them [deaf people] communicate onto the hearing world and empowers them to be more independent."

The device, which will cost less than $500, is not yet on the market, although the team is hoping to launch a smaller version later this year.

"It's a complex technology, it takes a lot of computational power," said Mr Dreger.

"And while we're very excited by it, we're taking our time to get it right."

The Sign device is one of a number of projects aimed at helping deaf people communicate more easily.

Another includes a glove fitted with sensors that convert sign language movements into text messages.
